newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. recommends rollover of Iraqi oil-for-food deal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. recommends rollover of Iraqi oil-for-food deal.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan on Monday recommended a six-month renewal of the "oil-for-food" deal for Iraq to help civilians survive under stringent trade sanctions, according to a draft report.

The current plan, which expires on June 7, calls for $2 billion worth of oil sales over six months so Baghdad can buy food and medicine for its people, suffering from sanctions imposed in August 1990 when Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait.

"In light of the experience gained in the implementation of the programme in the past six months and bearing in mind the continuing humanitarian crisis in Iraq, I recommend the renewal of the programme for a further period of six months," the report said.

The Security Council must still approve a rollover of the deal which went into effect on Dec. 10. The United States has not given its official position yet although U.S. sources believe Washington will agree to the renewal.
About two-thirds of the monies are for humanitarian supplies, with the remainder earmarked for compensation of Gulf War victims and the costs of destroying Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

In the Kurdish areas of the north, the report said that 19.3 percent of chldren under five were malnourished, of which 26 percent were chronically malnourished and four percent were acutely malnourished.

Annan did not recommend an increase in the oil sales but said the current food and nutrient supply was for a "basic survival level" of 2,030 calories a day compared to a desirable minimum of 2,500 calories per person.
But some of the foodstuffs lacked vitamins, particularly iron needed by pregnant woman.

Inadequacies also existed in such items as blankets, cooking utensils and heaters and proper educational materials, particularly to support the handicapped and street children as well as day care centres. In addition about $13.5 million is estimated by the U.N. Children's Fund to provide immunisation and health services as well as sanitation and clean water.

In the north where the United Nations has charge of much of the distribution, the report said the incursion by Turkey had not yet disturbed food distribution, except for one day but could do so if it continued or escalated.

Iraq has complained frequently that the council's procedures had prevented the supplies from reaching the country within a reasonable period of time while oil sales moved quickly. Annan agreed there had been delays.

Of the 630 applications for imports of humanitarian supplies to date, 574 were presented to the U.N. sanctions committee. Of this group 331 were approved, 191 were placed on hold, 14 were blocked, 24 were cancelled and 38 are pending.
